title: One forecaster with the optimal regret rate for every proper loss
formal: For each fixed number \(K\ge 2\) of outcomes, does there exist one randomized online forecaster A, not given the loss function, such that for every bounded proper loss \(\ell\) its worst-case expected regret satisfies \(R_{A},\ell (T)\le C_{\ell},K\cdot (1+R*_{\ell},K(T))\cdot (\log (T+2))^{c_{\ell},K}\) for all \(T\ge 1\), for some constants \(C_{\ell},K>0\) and \(c_{\ell},K\ge 0\) independent of T? Here \(R*_{\ell},K\) is the minimax regret achievable by a forecaster tailored to that particular loss. This spells out the source’s “optimal up to constant or logarithmic factors in T” target; the additive one covers losses with zero or bounded optimal regret.
why: Would establish whether a general-purpose probability forecaster can match every downstream user’s best possible learning rate without knowing that user’s loss. It refines universal sublinear regret into adaptation to the intrinsic difficulty of each scoring rule.
status_note: Full forecasting model, proven simultaneous bounds and concluding question checked with the June arXiv record and subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No loss-universal minimax-rate result or impossibility was located. The displayed minimax comparison makes the asymptotic target explicit.

progress.text: The paper simultaneously achieves logarithmic regret for smooth proper losses and nearly square-root regret for every bounded proper loss, leaving individual-rate optimality for all proper losses open.

sentences: One online forecaster must issue predictions before knowing which proper loss a downstream user cares about.
The question asks it to match each loss’s own optimal regret rate up to logarithmic factors in the horizon.
The benchmark is the best fixed probability prediction in hindsight, with expectation over the forecaster’s randomness.
The source already combines logarithmic regret for smooth losses with nearly square-root regret for all bounded proper losses.
The remaining task is to adapt to the individually optimal rate of every bounded proper loss.

references.title: Toward Simultaneously Optimal Regret in U-Calibration
references.authors: Rafael Frongillo, Haipeng Luo, Nishant A. Mehta, Jon Schneider
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 13; PDF page 13

definitions: The prediction space is the simplex \(\Delta _{K}=\{p\in \mathbb{R} ^{K}:p_{i}\ge 0,\sum p_{i}=1\}\). At round t, A chooses a possibly random \(\mathrm{P}_{t}\in \Delta _{K}\) from earlier revealed outcomes, then observes \(y_{t}\in \{e_{1},\ldots ,e_{K}\}\), where \(e_{i}\) is the ith unit vector. The adversary fixes \(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{T}\) in advance, knowing A but not its random bits. For a measurable loss \(\ell\):\(\Delta _{K}\times \{e_{1},\ldots ,e_{K}\}\to [- 1,1]\), propriety means \(E_{Y\sim p}\ell (p,Y)\le E_{Y\sim p}\ell (q,Y)\) for every \(p,q\in \Delta _{K}\); the minimizer need not be unique. Define \(Reg_{A},\ell (y_{1}:T)=E_{A}[\sum _{t=1}^{T} \ell (\mathrm{P}_{t},y_{t})]- \inf _{p\in \Delta _{K}}\sum _{t=1}^{T}\ell (p,y_{t})\). The expectation is over forecasting randomness, while the comparator is the best single fixed probability prediction in hindsight. Propriety makes the empirical outcome distribution a minimizing comparator. Set \(R_{A},\ell (T)=\sup _{y_{1}:T}Reg_{A},\ell (y_{1}:T)\), and \(R*_{\ell},K(T)=\inf _{B} R_{B},\ell (T)\), where B ranges over randomized online prediction strategies allowed to know \(\ell ,K\) and T. The desired A may know K and the horizon T, but its predictions are independent of which downstream loss is evaluated. Constants and logarithmic exponents may depend on the fixed loss and K; the asymptotic comparison is in T. This is an expected-regret comparison for each loss, not one simultaneous high-probability event over all losses. The question does not impose a particular polynomial running-time bound or a finite-precision implementation model; the target is the attainable online regret rate.
answer_criterion: Construct a loss-independent forecaster and prove the comparison for every bounded proper loss, or show that every such forecaster has some bounded proper loss for which its worst-case expected regret exceeds every allowed logarithmic-factor comparison with that loss’s minimax rate. Achieving \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{T})\) for all losses alone does not settle the question, because some individual losses admit logarithmic or smaller regret.

context_blocks.title: Different users judge the same forecast differently
context_blocks.text: A probability forecast can be used by many downstream decision makers. Proper losses reward reporting the true probability distribution in expectation, but different losses penalize mistakes differently. The forecaster must issue the same \(\mathrm{P}_{t}\) before knowing which user’s loss will be used.

context_blocks.title: Worst-case optimal for a class can still be poor for an easy loss
context_blocks.text: For squared loss, logarithmic regret is attainable. A general guarantee of order \(\sqrt{T}\) can therefore be much worse than a user could obtain with a loss-specific forecaster. The target adapts to each loss’s own difficulty, rather than just the hardest loss in the class.

context_blocks.title: One predictor already adapts to an important subclass
context_blocks.text: The paper gives one efficient algorithm with \(\widetilde{O}\)\((K^{5/4}\sqrt{T})\) regret for every bounded proper loss and \(O(\beta  \log  T+\beta \sqrt{K} \log  K)\) for bounded \(\beta\)-smooth proper losses. It also extends logarithmic guarantees to a broader relative-smoothness class. These are substantial simultaneous guarantees, but do not characterize every individual proper loss.

context_blocks.title: The comparator cannot change its forecast each round
context_blocks.text: The hindsight benchmark is one fixed probability vector p, chosen after all outcomes are known. Competing with a different optimal \(p_{t}\) on every round would be a much stronger and generally impossible target under arbitrary outcome sequences.

context_blocks.title: No common random event is being asserted
context_blocks.text: For each fixed loss, average regret over A’s own randomization must have the required rate against every fixed outcome sequence. The statement does not claim that a single realized random trajectory satisfies all loss bounds with high probability.
